Keep the kitchen layout consistent in all four panels so it clearly feels like the same place from different angles. Keep the wife’s silhouette rigid and vertical, and the husband’s silhouette elastic, floppy, and overlong. WHERE SHE IS

SHE STANDS AT THE STOVE WITH HER BACK TO CAMERA, in the middle of the picture, cooking. Her face is turned away and stays out of the picture for most of the shot. What we read is her back, her curlers, her shoulders, the dressing gown down to her calves, her slippers on the parquet.

SHE IS HAVING A LOVELY TIME, AND IT IS ALL IN HER HIPS

She is enjoying herself and she is moving to the music, and the movement lives BELOW HER WAIST.
HER HIPS SWING SIDE TO SIDE — over to one side, then over to the other, a good round unhurried swing, the whole seat of the dressing gown going with them, the hem swaying a beat behind. That swing is the biggest movement in the picture and it is what the shot is about.
Her weight goes with it: as her hips go one way her free heel lifts a little on the other side, and back again.
HER SHOULDERS ANSWER GENTLY, tipping the opposite way to her hips so her back reads as one soft S, and her head stays level on top of it all.
HER FREE HAND STAYS ON HER HIP and rides the swing. Her working hand keeps stirring over the pan the whole time, steady and unbothered.
THE TOWEL ON HER SHOULDER swings a beat behind everything else.
ALL OF IT HAPPENS FLAT IN THE PLANE OF THE PICTURE: she slides and tips from side to side, and her back stays square to camera the whole time.

WHAT HAPPENS

FIRST — SHE COOKS AND SHE SWAYS. Two full swings of the hips, easy and pleased with herself, stirring away, the kitchen warm and sunlit around her.
THEN — ONE FAT DROP FALLS ON HER. It comes down from the top edge of the frame and lands on her shoulder, right on the towel. She stops dead mid-swing, one hip still out to the side. Her stirring hand stops over the pan.
THEN — SHE LOOKS UP. Her head tips back so she is looking at the ceiling, and her free hand comes off her hip and goes up to touch the wet spot on her shoulder. She holds it there, puzzled rather than alarmed — mildly surprised, the way somebody is when a thing makes no sense yet.
THEN — MORE DROPS COME. Another lands, then another, then several at once from different places along the top of the frame: onto the counter beside her, onto the hob, onto the floor at her slippers, onto her curlers. Small dark wet marks appear where they land, and a few tiny droplets scatter off each one.
FINALLY — THE DRIPS KEEP COMING AND SHE KEEPS STARING UP. She stands there with her head back and her hand on her shoulder while the water goes on falling around her, and the shot holds like that to the last frame. The drips do not slow and they do not stop.

A hand-painted gouache EXPRESSION SHEET: nine heads of the same woman, side by side on a plain flat neutral grey backing, showing nine different expressions. In the manner of flat hand-painted 2D characters composited over a stylized 3D-rendered set character art.

REFERENCE
<<<c92623e6-3014-4e84-a99f-19e3e6a929b6>>> — THE WOMAN HERSELF. Her design, her outline, her proportions, her painted surface, her heavy face with its full cheeks, her long nose, her small mouth, her purple curlers pinned across her dark hair, her skin tone, the collar of her raspberry dressing gown at her neck. Every head on this sheet is that same head, drawn the same way, at the same size, from the same front-on angle. Only the expression differs.

THE LAYOUT
NINE HEADS IN A GRID: three rows of three, evenly spaced, each head the same size as every other, each with clear grey showing all round it. Each head is drawn from the neck up, front on, level, looking straight out of the picture. No head touches another and none of them overlaps.
Reading the grid left to right, top row first:
1. NEUTRAL — brows level and relaxed, lids at their ordinary opening, mouth a soft closed line. This is her resting face and the eight others are measured against it.
2. CONTENT — the outer corners of her mouth lift a little, her lower lids come up a fraction, her brows stay where they are. Quietly pleased.
3. PUZZLED — one brow lifts higher than the other, her mouth pulls a little to one side. She has noticed something that makes no sense.
4. FURY — her brows come down hard and draw together into a knot, her upper lids sit low so her eyes are narrowed, her mouth is a flat straight line.
5. INDIGNANT — her brows down but apart rather than knotted, her chin drawn in a fraction, her mouth pressed small and tight. Offended rather than enraged.
6. UNEASE — her brows up with THE INNER ENDS HIGHER THAN THE OUTER ONES, making a soft peak, her lids at their ordinary opening, her mouth small and a little downturned at the corners.
7. ALARM — her brows up and level, her lids up a little from ordinary, her mouth open just enough to show a dark line. Something has gone wrong and she has just understood it.
8. WEARY — her brows sagging outward and down at the ends, her upper lids heavy and low, her mouth a long flat line. Tired of all of it.
9. SOFTENING — her brows relaxed and level, her lower lids up a fraction, her mouth barely curved, her whole face let go. Giving in.

HOW BIG THE CHANGES ARE
ALL NINE ARE PLAYED SMALL. This character does everything with her brows and her eyelids, and her mouth takes only a little part. The whole range from her calmest face to her angriest is a matter of a few millimetres of brow and lid.
IN ALL NINE HEADS HER EYES KEEP THE SAME OPENING AND HER PUPILS KEEP THE SAME SIZE, and her pupils are aimed straight ahead in every one. What differs from head to head is the height and the angle of her brows, how far her upper lids sit, and the shape of her mouth.
Her jaw stays closed in eight of the nine, and opens only slightly in ALARM.
Her head keeps the same tilt in all nine: level, front on, square to the viewer.

HOW SHE IS PAINTED
Soft opaque gouache: brush marks visible across her skin and her hair, a hand-drawn contour around each head, dark ink accents in a few creases, a light paper grain inside the fill, her colour sitting in even flat areas with clean painted edges between them. Matte and quiet, with soft mid tones, gentle darks and a small tonal range: closer to a book illustration than to a poster. Every one of the nine heads is painted in the same paint, on the same paper, with the same brush, and they belong to one drawing.

THE BACKING
Behind the grid, one flat even neutral grey, edge to edge, with nothing on it: no floor, no wall, no room, no shadow under the heads, no gradient, no texture, no writing and no numbers. The heads sit alone on it as cut-outs, with clear grey between them and clear grey around the whole grid.

Her own warm painted skin, dark ink-blue hair, lilac curlers, the raspberry #78203a of her collar in its muted painted form. Warm pale ochre light #e8c088 as the general key of the paint.

WHAT IS GOING ON INSIDE HER, AND HOW IT SHOWS
She has just been grabbed and kissed by a corpse and she is furious about it. She wants to be out of this flat immediately.
BUT SHE IS NOT GOING TO GIVE ANYONE THE SATISFACTION OF SEEING THAT. She is leaving with her dignity in one piece, and the whole performance is her holding herself together.
IT SHOWS IN HOW TIGHTLY SHE IS HELD, and nowhere else. Her back is very straight. Her shoulders are squared and pulled back. Her chin is up. Her hands are closed and pressed against her sides. Everything about her is a fraction too composed, too upright, too correct — the stiffness of somebody who has decided to walk out properly.
AND IT ALMOST BREAKS. Her walk is a shade quicker than a dignified walk should be, and her steps are a little too even, as though she is counting them. Once or twice her stride nearly runs away with her before she takes it back. That flicker between fleeing and marching is the shot.
NOTHING ABOUT HER IS THEATRICAL: she does not stamp, does not gesture, does not shake and does not hurry openly. It is all in the tightness of the hold.

WHERE SHE IS FROM THE FIRST FRAME
SHE IS ALREADY IN THE PICTURE when the shot opens. WHAT HAPPENS

FIRST — she stands there for a beat with her back to us, dead straight, gathering herself.

THEN — SHE WALKS AT THE DOOR. She crosses towards the open doorway, drawn as three or four held positions, each sitting still for a beat and replaced by the next in a single step. The steps come evenly and a shade too fast, her shoulders squared, the hem of her gown snapping behind her at each one. Her size on screen stays as it was.

THEN — SHE STOPS AT THE BASIN, and the stop is abrupt: she pulls up hard beside it, everything about her arriving at once. HER HEAD TIPS DOWN so she is looking at it lying on the floor. She holds that. In the hold her shoulders come up a fraction and settle again — the one moment the composure slips, and she takes it straight back.

THEN — SHE TURNS AND LOOKS BACK. Her head comes round over her shoulder towards the LEFT of the picture, back the way she came, and HER FACE APPEARS in the frame for the first time. Her body stays where it is, still squared at the door. She holds that look.
HER FACE IS COLD AND OFFENDED, HELD IN: her brows down but apart rather than knotted, her chin drawn in a fraction, her mouth pressed small and tight, her lids at their ordinary opening. It is the face of somebody who has been insulted and has decided to say nothing about it.

Each shadow shape has a hard painted edge on the outside and a soft gradient inside the
shape, in a darker tone of his own colour. Three to four tonal steps across each
surface.

HOW HE SITS IN THE ROOM
He keeps his own flat local colours and stays outside the room's light: the kitchen's
daylight, its reflections and its cast shadows belong to the render and stay on the
render.
Screen overlaps: the raised knee crosses in front of the stretched leg and covers part
of it; the near forearm crosses in front of his chest; his shoulder covers the base of
his neck; the yellow bucket stands in front of his stretched leg and cuts across the
slipper. In each one the near shape stays whole and the far shape is cut by it.
His contour is a fine hand-drawn line of one even weight all the way round. Each hand
keeps four digits held together.
Lying down, he spans from the left edge of the stove across to the yellow bucket, and
his whole figure is inside the frame.

HIS SHADOW
One separate flat painted shape on the parquet, a soft-edged silhouette filled evenly
with a single darker tone of the boards' own colour, nothing inside it. It meets him
along the line where his shoulders, back, hips, stretched leg, planted foot and outflung
hand touch the floor, and opens into clear floor under the raised knee and under the
lifted elbow. It stays flat on the boards, light in tone, in the same gentle weight as
the shadows already in the plate.

STYLE
Mixed-media 2D-over-3D in the manner of flat hand-painted 2D characters composited over a stylized 3D-rendered set: flat
hand-painted gouache cut-out characters over smooth matte toy-like CGI with soft
rounded edges. Matte opaque gouache, visible paper tooth, crisp edges. 4:3.
